summary: Valproic acid is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic used for absence and complex partial seizures, bipolar disorder and migraine prophylaxis. It carries boxed warnings for hepatotoxicity (highest risk in children under 2), teratogenicity (neural tube defects, decreased IQ, neurodevelopmental disorders) and life-threatening pancreatitis. Dosing starts at 10-15 mg/kg/day and is titrated to effect or 60 mg/kg/day. Requires monitoring of LFTs, platelets, ammonia and drug levels.
indications: Monotherapy and adjunctive therapy of complex partial seizures
Sole and adjunctive therapy of simple and complex absence seizures
Adjunctive therapy in patients with multiple seizure types that include absence seizures
(Divalproex forms also indicated for acute mania in bipolar disorder and migraine prophylaxis)

dosage.n: Max 60 mg/kg/day; safety above not established
Reduced clearance and protein binding; monitor intake
If total >250 mg/day, give in divided doses

admin: Administer orally with food if GI upset occurs; swallow capsules/tablets whole (do not chew delayed-release)
Initiate at low mg/kg dose and titrate at weekly intervals to response or tolerability
Obtain baseline liver function tests and monitor frequently, especially in the first 6 months
Use as sole agent and with extreme caution in children under 2 years (highest hepatotoxicity risk)
Measure ammonia level if unexplained lethargy, vomiting or mental status change occurs
moa: Valproic acid dissociates to the valproate ion in the GI tract. Its precise antiepileptic mechanism is not established but is thought to involve increased brain concentrations of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and modulation of voltage-gated sodium and calcium (T-type) channels, reducing neuronal excitability.

absolute: Hepatic disease or significant hepatic dysfunction
Known mitochondrial disorders from POLG mutations (e.g., Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome)
Suspected POLG-related disorder in children under 2 years
Pregnancy / non-contracepting women of childbearing potential (migraine prophylaxis)
relative: Women of childbearing potential for epilepsy/bipolar unless other therapies inadequate

preg: Teratogenic. Causes neural tube defects, decreased IQ, neurodevelopmental disorders and other major congenital malformations, occurring very early in pregnancy. Contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy. For epilepsy/bipolar, do not use in pregnant women or women of childbearing potential unless other treatments have failed; use effective contraception. Folic acid supplementation is advised.
lact: Valproate is excreted in breast milk at low concentrations; it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Monitor the infant for jaundice, unusual drowsiness, poor feeding and bleeding.
renal: No formal dose adjustment, but reduced renal function alters protein binding and increases free valproate; monitor free (unbound) levels and clinical response. Valproate is dialyzable.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatic disease or significant hepatic dysfunction. Fatal hepatotoxicity can occur, usually within the first 6 months; monitor liver tests closely and discontinue for suspected/diagnosed significant hepatic dysfunction.

major: Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem) - markedly reduce valproate levels and seizure control; avoid
Lamotrigine - valproate doubles lamotrigine levels (serious rash/SJS risk); reduce lamotrigine dose
moderate: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine) - altered levels of both drugs
Aspirin - displaces valproate, raising free level
Rufinamide, ethosuximide, clonazepam, diazepam - altered levels
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce GI irritation; food can delay but not reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression and increased hepatotoxicity risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine ketone tests; alters thyroid function tests; can elevate ammonia and liver enzymes.

emergency: Acute hepatic failure (malaise, vomiting, facial edema, loss of seizure control)

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline and frequently, especially in first 6 months
CBC with platelets and coagulation tests before therapy and periodically
Serum ammonia if lethargy, vomiting or mental status changes
Valproate plasma levels (typical therapeutic 50-100 mcg/mL) and free level in renal/hepatic impairment
Signs/symptoms of pancreatitis; pregnancy status in women of childbearing potential
counsel: Take every day as prescribed; report jaundice, severe abdominal pain, unusual bruising/bleeding or confusion immediately
Women of childbearing potential: use effective contraception and discuss serious fetal risks before/during use
Do not stop abruptly (risk of seizures); avoid alcohol
Report new or worsening depression, agitation or thoughts of self-harm
Take folic acid if of childbearing potential; carry seizure/medication information
pk: Anticonvulsant effect over days as levels build
Steady state in 1-4 days; BID dosing common
pearls: BOXED WARNINGS: hepatotoxicity (highest in children <2), teratogenicity (neural tube defects, low IQ), and life-threatening pancreatitis
Carbapenems can drastically lower valproate levels - avoid combination
Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels - halve lamotrigine dosing and titrate slowly
Check ammonia for unexplained encephalopathy even with normal LFTs; topiramate increases this risk
Highly protein bound - measure free level when albumin is low or in renal failure
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose. Do not double the next dose. Maintaining steady levels is important for seizure control.
overdose: Overdose may cause somnolence, heart block, deep coma and hypernatremia; fatalities have occurred. Provide supportive care with attention to urine output. Hemodialysis (or hemodialysis plus hemoperfusion) can significantly remove drug given high free fraction. Naloxone has reversed CNS depression but may also reverse antiepileptic effect - use cautiously in epilepsy. L-carnitine may help hyperammonemia.
